name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Sunday 2 October 1983

clue.text: Keeps sun off father, artist and most of my boot bottom

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing what the noun does

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its final letter, so one letter is dropped

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist
the sole is the underneath of a boot

explanation.surface: Dad, a painter and a worn-down boot sole somehow all shading someone from the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: SOLE loses its last letter to leave SOL, giving PARASOL.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasol is a light umbrella carried to give shade, so its whole job is blocking sunlight.

clue.text: Honest prig in broken hut

indicators.note: something broken has its parts knocked out of their original order
one word sits inside the other, which wraps round it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A self-righteous person holed up in a ramshackle shed, perhaps praised for honesty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken hut' reads as a wrecked shed, but only the little word's letters are broken, and the other word then sits inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: An upright person is morally straight and trustworthy, a standard synonym for honest.

clue.text: The road in could give us a dry view, perhaps

indicators.note: the letters could produce something else once they are rearranged, which is what this phrase hints
perhaps admits the result is one possible version of the letters, another hint at rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A road leading into a parched landscape might offer a bleak, dusty outlook.
explanation.definitionFit: A driveway is the private road leading in from the street to a house.

clue.text: In my garden I also hide my negations

indicators.note: something hidden sits concealed among the other letters of the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run across letters 4-10 of 'garden I also'

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to burying their refusals out in the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A denial is a statement that something is not so, the same thing as a negation.

clue.text: Might make Eve rant, but he 'Only fades away"

indicators.note: the letters might be made into something else, which signals rearranging them

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An old man so quiet that he would hardly provoke Eve to rage.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes the old song: 'Old soldiers never die, they only fade away'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song line is about old soldiers, and an old soldier is a veteran.

clue.text: Pare the wood while get ting round the non-drinker

indicators.note: getting round means wrapping about something else, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: taken as written
TT, teetotal, marks someone who drinks no alcohol

explanation.surface: Carving a stick while trying to get around someone who won't drink.
explanation.walkthrough: TT stands for teetotal, a convention for a non-drinker. 'get ting' is the scan's split of 'getting'.
explanation.definitionFit: To whittle is to shave thin strips off a piece of wood with a knife.

clue.text: Kind of hay-mask used for Eastern maidenly modesty

definitions.note: the thing used for modesty stands for the modesty

indicators.note: a kind of something is a version of it, here a version with its letters reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: A face covering of hay worn by modest women in the East.
explanation.definitionFit: A yashmak is the veil some Muslim women wear in public to keep the face covered out of modesty.

clue.text: Senate leader has more than enough for this taste

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
ample means plentiful, more than enough

explanation.surface: The Senate's leader has had plenty, so this taste is all they want.
explanation.definitionFit: A sample is a small taste of food or drink, and to taste can mean to sample.

clue.text: R.L.S. is not confusing these air passages

indicators.note: confusing something mixes it up, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written, stops ignored

explanation.surface: A denial that Robert Louis Stevenson (R.L.S.) was confused about breathing.
explanation.walkthrough: R.L.S. is the writer Robert Louis Stevenson, but here it is just three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The nostrils are the openings of the nose through which breath passes in and out.

clue.text: Isle where, in retrospect, it returns twice about half laugh

indicators.note: something that returns goes back the way it came, so the word runs backwards
looking in retrospect is looking backwards, so the half laugh is read the other way
about means around, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: the little word backwards, used twice
a laugh is HA-HA; half of it is one HA

explanation.surface: A holiday island where, looking back, someone keeps half-laughing about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first copy of the reversed little word goes round the half laugh; the second simply follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia in the South Pacific.

clue.text: Get manager a tumbler of water with blue flower in it

indicators.note: the answer is in it, sitting within the letters of the run of words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third
surface padding, part of the scene only
surface padding, part of the scene only

explanation.surface: Fetching the boss a glass of water with a blue bloom floating in it.
explanation.walkthrough: AGERATUM is concealed in 'manAGER A TUMbler'; 'Get' and 'of water with' are only part of the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Ageratum, also called flossflower, is a garden plant grown for its fluffy blue blooms.

clue.text: These, of meat, the cockney walks on

definitions.text: These, of meat, the cockney walks on

blocks.note: surface: dishes of meat
setter's reading: Cockney rhyming slang, where these of meat rhymes with feet, the things one walks on

explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang (London street slang), 'plates of meat' means feet, often cut to just 'plates'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyming-slang phrase stands for the feet, which a Londoner walks on.

clue.text: Quietly curves architecturally and renders dry

blocks.note: p, piano, is the musical marking for quietly
arches are the curved structures of a building

explanation.surface: An architect's gentle curves somehow leave a building dried out.
explanation.definitionFit: To parch something is to make it thoroughly dry, as the sun does to land.

clue.text: Lawless rule puts structural part of 11 Down in any surroundings

indicators.note: one part goes in, and the other forms surroundings around it

blocks.note: taken as written
11 Down's curves are arches; one of them is an arch

explanation.surface: A state without laws sets architectural elements anywhere it likes.
explanation.walkthrough: '11 Down' points at another answer, PARCHES, whose wordplay used arches; one arch is the structural part meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchy is a state of disorder with no government or laws, literally rule by nobody.

clue.text: One who reveals is former artist's model

blocks.note: ex means formerly
a model poses for an artist

explanation.surface: A whistleblower turns out to have once sat as a painter's model.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who exposes a secret or a scandal is an exposer, one who lays it bare.

clue.text: Not below on a group of 52

blocks.note: taken as written
a deck of playing cards holds 52

explanation.surface: A cryptic count: not underneath, on top of a set of fifty-two.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, being on deck means up top in the open, not down below.

clue.text: Two 16 terms to infest

blocks.note: 16 Down is cricket; an over and a run are two of its terms

explanation.surface: Two sporting words used to describe pests swarming a place.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, an over is a set of six balls and a run is a single point scored.
explanation.definitionFit: Pests that infest a place overrun it, spreading through every part.

clue.text: Not the brightest duets involving two learners

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so one piece is drawn inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the learner-driver plate, so two of them

explanation.surface: Pairs of singers bringing in two beginners are hardly the brightest performers.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion gives the right letters but in the wrong order at the end, and nothing signals a final shuffle; the setter's wordplay is loose here.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull means dim or lacking brightness, so dullest is the least bright of all.

clue.text: A game for a chirpy creature

blocks.note: first meaning: the bat-and-ball sport
second meaning: an insect known for its chirping

explanation.walkthrough: 'chirpy' sounds like cheerful, but it is literal: the insect chirps.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names the bat-and-ball sport and the jumping insect that chirps at night.

clue.text: Concerning a bookie, anger makes us aim high again

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
taken as written
SP, starting price, is the bookmaker's odds at the off
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Fury at a bookmaker spurs us on to set our sights high once more.
explanation.walkthrough: SP for starting price is the odds a bookie pays out at, a racing abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to aim high; doing it a second time is to re-aspire.

clue.text: Tiler returns carrying cent for the widow

indicators.note: something that returns heads back, so the word runs in the opposite direction
carrying something means holding it inside

blocks.note: taken as written
c is the abbreviation for cent

explanation.surface: A roofer comes back carrying small change for a woman whose husband has died.
explanation.definitionFit: Relict is an old legal word for a widow, the one left behind by a husband's death.

clue.text: Pedlar he struck in a mix up

indicators.note: a mix-up is a jumbling, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A street seller lashed out during a scuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A huckster is a hawker selling small goods, often pushily, just as a pedlar does.

clue.text: The coat for Northern Ire land'

blocks.note: first meaning: a long, heavy overcoat with a cape
second meaning: the historic province often used as a name for Northern Ireland

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ire land' is the scan's split of 'Ireland'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulster overcoat was first made in Belfast, the capital of the province the same name refers to.

clue.text: Ray knits components fora a big plane

indicators.note: taking something into its components breaks it apart so it can be rebuilt differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Ray knitting parts for a large aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: Skytrain was Laker Airways' cheap transatlantic airliner service of the late 1970s; 'fora' is the scan's 'for a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Skytrain was the name given to wide-bodied jet services, a big passenger aircraft run cheaply.
